Longjawed galaxias (Galaxias prognathus) occupies a restricted range within the braided river systems of New Zealand, where it exhibits a life history strategy tightly coupled to cool, well-oxygenated waters. Field surveys indicate that newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 3.1e-3 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.1e-3 grams], a value consistent with the tiny, demersal eggs from which they hatch. This lecithotrophic stage relies entirely on endogenous reserves, and the transition to exogenous feeding occurs shortly after the mouth opens. The species is relatively short-lived under natural conditions; mark-recapture studies in the wild have documented a maximum lifespan of approximately 4.5 years [am = approximately 4.5 years], though this figure is sensitive to at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]thermal regime. The extreme longevity observed in nature underscores the physiological constraints imposed by the species' cold-water habitat, where metabolic rates are depressed and somatic growth proceeds slowly.

Reproductive output in Galaxias prognathus is modest but highly seasonal, reflecting the energetic constraints of a small-bodied galaxiid inhabiting a highly stochastic environment. Females reach puberty, defined by the onset of vitellogenesis and the first appearance of maturing oocytes, at a total length of 6.5 centimeters [Lp = 6.5 centimeters]. Spawning typically occurs during the austral spring and early summer, when water temperatures rise. The daily egg production rate at 8 °C [T = 8 °C] was estimated at 0.767 eggs, a rate that reflects a trade-off between egg size and fecundity. This daily production rate translates into a substantial seasonal investment, as females spawn repeatedly over several weeks.

The size structure of Longjawed galaxias populations reflects a pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate body length, a pattern commonly observed in galaxiid fishes where females attain larger sizes. The ultimate total length for females has been measured at 8.7 centimeters [Li = 8.7 centimeters], a value that represents the asymptotic body size reached after several years of slow growth. Males, by contrast, achieve a smaller ultimate total length of 7.7 centimeters [Li = 7.7 centimeters], a difference that likely arises from differential energy expenditure during the reproductive season. Field-caught individuals approaching these maximum lengths are typically older than four years and exhibit thickened opercular bones and well-developed fin rays, signs of advanced age. The growth trajectory itself is strongly temperature-dependent; a separate laboratory cohort reared at 19 °C [T = 19 °C] attained these ultimate sizes more rapidly than wild fish.

Age at first reproduction in Galaxias prognathus is tightly linked to the attainment of a threshold body size rather than a fixed chronological age. Using a laboratory rearing experiment conducted at 8 °C [T = 8 °C], researchers observed that females began spawning once they reached a total length of 6.5 centimeters. This size-based threshold likely reflects the minimum body cavity volume required to accommodate a clutch of yolked oocytes. The protracted maturation period, spanning one to two years depending on local thermal conditions, represents a significant investment in somatic growth before the onset of reproductive activity. Comparative data from congeneric species indicate that this size at puberty is typical for galaxiids inhabiting cool, oligotrophic streams, where food resources are seasonally pulsed and growth rates are slow.

The combination of a very small birth mass (3.1e-3 grams) [Wwb = 3.1e-3 grams] and a maximum lifespan of 4.5 years [am = 4.5 years] at 19 °C [T = 19 °C] places Galaxias prognathus among the shorter-lived galaxiids with a high reproductive turnover. The species' reproductive physiology, including an egg production rate of 0.767 offspring per day at 8 °C [T = 8 °C], appears finely tuned to the brief windows of optimal thermal conditions that characterize its native habitat, where rapid early growth and early maturation are favored over extended longevity.
